title: Class-Balanced Softmax: A Bayes Theory-Based Method for Long-Tailed Recognition
abstract: Deep learning models using traditional softmax classifiers have achieved remarkable success in various classification tasks. However, their performance degrades significantly on imbalanced datasets. Although Balanced Softmax is widely adopted as a state-of-the-art rebalancing method, it possesses inherent limitations, such as yielding disproportionately lower testing accuracy for tail classes. To mitigate these shortcomings, we propose the Class-Balanced Softmax (CBS). Rooted in a theoretical Bayesian framework and a heuristic power-law assumption, the CBS is a simple logit adjustment that is computationally inexpensive and easily integrated into existing pipelines. Furthermore, we characterise a fundamental phenomenon in models trained on imbalanced data, termed the preference issue, wherein models exhibit higher training error and a larger generalisation gap for classes with limited data. To quantify this issue, we introduce a novel metric and demonstrate that CBS effectively mitigates the preference issue. Extensive experiments on large-scale benchmarks show that CBS is highly scalable and outperforms existing methods, including Balanced Softmax.

Since then, deep learning models have achieved impressive performance in various computer vision tasks, including image classification [ 17 , 14 , 8 ] and image segmentation [ 13 ] . This paper focuses on image classification, which plays a crucial role in various tasks, including object detection [ 28 ] and instance segmentation [ 13 ] . In the image classification community, the datasets under investigation often suffer from imbalance, i.e., some classes have significantly more training samples than others [ 27 , 12 ] . Often, the training data exhibits a long-tailed distribution [ 27 , 12 ] . Following the existing literature, we use the terms head classes , medium classes and tail classes to split the classes in a given dataset into three groups. Head classes have the largest number of training samples per class, while tail classes have the lowest. It has been observed that models trained on imbalanced data tend to provide a higher recall on the testing data for head classes compared to tail classes [ 37 ] , referred to as the imbalanced testing performance . This paper focuses on imbalanced classification. The goal is to mitigate the impact of imbalanced data on the model training and ensure the model achieves high accuracy for all classes on the testing data. To handle imbalanced classification, a variety of methods have been proposed in the existing literature [ 33 ] . In general, the methods can be categorised into four types. (1) Rebalancing methods [ 3 , 25 , 35 ] : rebalancing methods aim to mitigate the impact of the imbalanced training data on model training. This is the key issue to be addressed in the field of imbalanced learning. As we discuss in Section 2 , the existing rebalancing methods often rely on restrictive theoretical assumptions or reduce training data diversity, which limits their performance. (2) Representation learning methods [ 29 , 6 , 26 , 19 ] : these methods focus on designing the model structure or loss function to enable the model to use the available data more effectively for training and thus improve the quality of representations. This will improve the model performance for all the classes. It is particularly important for tail classes, which have few training samples. However, these methods typically require additional trainable parameters and still rely on rebalancing methods as their classifier [ 29 , 6 , 26 ] . (3) Data augmentation [ 4 , 36 , 31 , 1 ] : these methods aim to increase the diversity of training data and are commonly applied as a default setup during image preprocessing. (4) Fixed linear classifiers [ 34 , 24 ] : the term classifier here refers to the last linear layer in the deep learning models [ 15 ] . The methods of this type generate values for the linear classifier weights and fix them to avoid the models expressing their preference towards head classes via the linear classifier weights. However, it is challenging to generate high-quality values for the weights [ 34 ] . To address the challenges in imbalanced classification, in this paper, we make three contributions to the imbalanced learning community, as follows. • Based on a theoretical Bayesian framework and heuristic power-law functions, we propose Class-Balanced Softmax (CBS) for imbalanced classification. CBS is a simple, computationally inexpensive logit adjustment method that can be seamlessly integrated into existing deep learning pipelines with negligible computational overhead and zero additional trainable parameters. Specifically, CBS introduces a parameterised power-law calibration hyperparameter, β ≥ 0 \beta\geq 0 , which modifies the raw logit z n ​ c z_{nc} output by the model for sample n n and class c c to z n ​ c + β ​ log ⁡ | 𝒩 c | z_{nc}+\beta\log|\mathcal{N}_{c}| (see Eq. 27 ), where | 𝒩 c | |\mathcal{N}_{c}| represents the training sample count in class c c . This formulation directly generalises Balanced Softmax, which represents a rigid special case when β = 1 \beta=1 . • To the best of our knowledge, this work is the first to characterise the preference issue as an inherent model symptom that provides a more fundamental insight into the aforementioned imbalanced testing performance of models trained on imbalanced data. This issue manifests as a disproportionately higher training error and larger generalisation gap for tail classes compared to head classes. To quantify this issue, we formulate a novel metric, referred to as model imbalance level ( I I ), and demonstrate that our proposed CBS mitigates the preference issue more effectively than state-of-the-art methods across diverse benchmarks. • Extensive experiments are conducted on various long-tailed benchmarks, including large-scale datasets such as ImageNet-LT (1000 classes) [ 20 ] , iNaturalist2018 (8142 classes) [ 27 ] and an LVIS-based dataset with extreme imbalance [ 12 ] . The results demonstrate that CBS is highly scalable and outperforms existing methods, including the state-of-the-art Balanced Softmax [ 25 ] . Furthermore, we reveal the fundamental limitations of softmax-based models in imbalanced settings through gradient-based theoretical analysis and empirical validation. This paper is organised as follows. Section 2 discusses the representative existing rebalancing methods. Section 3 studies the impact of imbalanced training data on the gradients and model performance. Section 4 presents our CBS . Section 5 provides experimental results, which confirm our analysis and demonstrate the performance of our CBS . Section 6 concludes the work. 2 Related work Rebalancing methods aim to mitigate the impact of the sample number difference between classes on the model. The existing rebalancing methods include mainly three types: resampling-based methods, reweighting-based methods and post-hoc correction methods. Both resampling-based methods and reweighting-based methods are applied for model training, while the post-hoc correction methods are applied only during the classification decisions. Resampling-based methods When training a model, samples are first selected, and then the selected samples are fed into the model for training. Resampling-based methods aim to balance the number of samples selected for each class. Undersampling and oversampling are the two most classic resampling methods [ 38 ] . Undersampling is no longer attractive due to inefficient training data use. By contrast, oversampling remains popular and was referred to as class-balanced sampling by [ 15 ] . It is simple to implement and provides decent performance. [ 15 ] also discussed different sampling methods and proposed the decoupled training framework, which has been applied in many later studies [ 33 ] . The Classifier Re-training (cRT) proposed by [ 15 ] combines class-balanced sampling and decoupled training. Resampling-based methods rebalance the training data at the expense of reducing data diversity. However, as demonstrated by [ 15 ] , maintaining maximum data diversity is essential for achieving high-quality representation learning in long-tailed recognition. By reducing training data diversity, resampling-based methods often compromise the learned representations and limit overall performance. Reweighting-based methods Reweighting methods are designed by incorporating weights into the loss function. These weights can be assigned per sample, per class, or even per group of classes. Focal Loss [ 18 ] is one of the earliest reweighting-based methods, with weights calculated for each sample based on its softmax output. Samples with lower prediction probabilities are assigned higher weights. Consequently, this approach is often referred to as hard sample mining. While tail classes typically contain a higher proportion of hard samples, head classes also contain a significant number of them, which limits the rebalancing effect of Focal Loss. Most reweighting methods determine weights based on the number of training samples per class. Representative works include [ 15 , 3 , 25 ] . In [ 3 ] , the authors proposed Label-Distribution-Aware Margin (LDAM) . However, as noted by [ 25 ] , LDAM is derived under a binary classification setup and may not be inherently suited for multi-class classification. Balanced Softmax [ 25 ] currently remains a state-of-the-art rebalancing method. Nevertheless, models trained with Balanced Softmax still exhibit imbalanced testing performance, where head classes maintain higher testing recall than tail classes. This discrepancy becomes more pronounced as the training data imbalance increases, contradicting the theoretical expectations of the method and stemming from specific assumptions made during its derivation. We provide a detailed discussion of these limitations in Appendix G . The logit-adjustment method introduced by [ 22 ] shares a similar shortcoming. Beyond per-class reweighting, [ 5 ] proposed Residual Learning for Long-tailed Recognition (ResLT) , which assigns higher weights to tail classes in the loss function and incorporates the post-hoc τ \tau -norm correction [ 15 ] . While ResLT achieves competitive results, it requires a significant number of additional trainable parameters and structural modifications to adapt to datasets with different imbalance levels. Post-hoc correction methods The τ \tau -norm method, proposed by [ 15 ] , is based on the observation that models trained on imbalanced data exhibit larger norms for linear classifier weights corresponding to head classes than those for tail classes. To address this, τ \tau -norm normalises the classifier weights using a hyperparameter τ \tau . A key limitation of this approach is that these normalised weights are often far from the optimal configuration for the learned features; consequently, the performance gains remain limited. Another prominent post-hoc correction strategy is the logit-adjustment method introduced by [ 22 ] . This approach shifts the output of the linear classifier by an amount proportional to the class-wise sample counts. Similar to τ \tau -norm, adjusting logits after training forces a shift in the decision boundary to mitigate the preference issue. However, the model parameters are not optimised in conjunction with this adjusted boundary, therefore, often remain suboptimal, which limits the overall effectiveness of the method. 3 Impact of imbalanced training data on model training In a standard deep learning model for object classification, each sample n n is compressed using a backbone, e.g., ResNet [ 14 ] as a vector 𝒉 n \boldsymbol{h}_{n} , which is commonly referred to as a feature vector or representation in the literature [ 2 ] . The preference issue A model trained on imbalanced data exhibits an inherent preference issue, where tail classes suffer from significantly higher training error and a larger generalisation gap than head classes. High training error indicates severe underfitting (low training recall), while the generalisation gap represents the relative percentage drop from training to testing recall. This phenomenon is illustrated in Figure 1 using a ResNet50 [ 14 ] with a standard softmax classifier on ImageNet-LT (see Section 5.2 for detailed configuration). As shown, head classes maintain high recall across both training and testing sets, whereas tail class recall on the test set drops to nearly half of its training value—a far more severe relative degradation than observed in head classes. Figure 1: The preference issue observed in the model trained on ImageNet-LT: significantly higher training error and larger generalisation gaps for tail classes. Solid lines represent average recall across class groups on training data. Dashed lines represent testing recall. Existing literature often attributes the poor performance of deep learning models for long-tailed recognition to the discrepancy between imbalanced training and an assumed balanced testing distribution [ 25 ] . While imbalanced training data is the root cause of performance degradation, we find the issue to be fundamentally independent of the testing data distribution, which in many real-world scenarios, such as the LVIS dataset [ 12 ] , remains unknown and is itself often imbalanced. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to reveal the preference issue as an inherent model characteristic caused by training on imbalanced data. This preference issue manifests as a structural imbalance in the model’s internal behaviour and persists regardless of the testing distribution. We believe that the preference issue provides a more fundamental insight into the nature of the long-tailed recognition problem. (27) The CBS , as formulated in Eq. 27 , is a computationally efficient logit adjustment that integrates seamlessly into existing deep learning pipelines with negligible overhead and no additional trainable parameters. Moreover, CBS fundamentally generalises Balanced Softmax, which emerges as a rigid special case when β = 1 \beta=1 . While Balanced Softmax applies a fixed additive logit shift of log ⁡ | 𝒩 c | \log|\mathcal{N}_{c}| based on class frequencies, CBS introduces the power-law hyperparameter β \beta to expand this modification to β ​ log ⁡ | 𝒩 c | \beta\log|\mathcal{N}_{c}| . This parameterised flexibility allows for dynamic calibration of class-wise gradient signals during back-propagation. Consequently, CBS maintains the computational efficiency of Balanced Softmax while proving more effective at mitigating the model preference issue, as demonstrated in Sec. 5 . Furthermore, although this paper focuses on imbalanced classification, CBS can be readily extended to other downstream tasks, such as long-tailed instance segmentation and object detection [ 12 ] . Interpretation of the CBS regarding gradients According to Theorem 4.2 , the CBS operates based on the relation between p ​ ( y = c ) p(y=c) , p ^ ​ ( y = c ) \hat{p}(y=c) , ϕ n ​ c \phi_{nc} and ϕ ^ n ​ c \hat{\phi}_{nc} . From the perspective of Eq. 6 , the additional term log ⁡ | 𝒩 c | β \log|\mathcal{N}_{c}|^{\beta} and log ⁡ | 𝒩 d | β \log|\mathcal{N}_{d}|^{\beta} in the CBS increases z n ​ c z_{nc} for head classes and reduces z n ​ c z_{nc} for tail classes during model training. This adjustment reduces the rewards and increases the penalties for head classes, while it increases the rewards and reduces the penalties for tail classes. This leads to more balanced gradients during the back-propagation for model training, thus mitigating the development of the preference issue. 5 Experiments This section details the experimental evaluation of the proposed CBS .
